clinicalPearls: Arises on a background of coeliac disease, often in patients with refractory coeliac disease type II, and usually presents in adults of northern European origin
Common presentations include abdominal pain, weight loss, and recurrence of malabsorptive symptoms despite a gluten-free diet, or an acute surgical picture of bowel perforation or obstruction
The jejunum is the most frequent site; tumours are often multifocal with ulceration and may present as multiple ulcers rather than a single mass
Neoplastic cells derive from intraepithelial T-lymphocytes and typically express CD3 and CD103, with variable CD30 and cytotoxic markers, and characteristically lack CD8 and CD56 in the classic form
Adjacent mucosa usually shows villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and an abnormal intraepithelial lymphocyte population confirming the enteropathy link
Distinguish from monomorphic epitheliotropic intestinal T-cell lymphoma, which is not coeliac-associated and expresses CD8 and CD56
Association with the coeliac-related HLA-DQ2/DQ8 genotype underpins the disease
reference.pathophysiology: Enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma develops from intraepithelial T-lymphocytes of the small intestine in the setting of long-standing coeliac disease. Chronic gluten-driven mucosal immune activation, particularly in refractory coeliac disease type II, gives rise to an aberrant, clonal intraepithelial lymphocyte population that has lost normal surface T-cell antigens. Accumulation of genetic changes, including alterations in the JAK-STAT signalling pathway, drives progression from this precursor state to overt lymphoma. The tumour cells retain gut-homing characteristics such as CD103 expression, and their transmural, ulcerating growth accounts for the high rate of perforation.
additionalDifferentials: Refractory coeliac disease type II without overt lymphoma
Crohn's disease or other inflammatory bowel disease with ulceration
Infective or ischaemic ulceration of the small intestine
additionalInvestigations: Endoscopic or surgical biopsy with immunohistochemistry (CD3, CD103, CD30, CD8, CD56) and cytotoxic markers
T-cell receptor clonality analysis on tumour and background mucosa
Coeliac serology and HLA-DQ2/DQ8 typing to confirm the enteropathy background
Video capsule endoscopy or enteroscopy to map multifocal small-bowel disease
Cross-sectional imaging (CT or MRI enterography) and PET for staging
Bone marrow examination and assessment of nutritional and metabolic status
redFlags: Signs of bowel perforation or peritonitis requiring urgent surgical assessment
Rapidly worsening malabsorption with profound weight loss and hypoalbuminaemia
Refractory coeliac disease failing to respond to a strict gluten-free diet, signalling possible progression
reference.prognosis: The outlook is poor, with frequent presentation as a surgical emergency, high relapse rates, and limited tolerance of intensive therapy owing to malnutrition; consolidation with autologous stem-cell transplant is used in fit patients.
pitfalls: Attributing recurrent symptoms to dietary non-adherence and delaying investigation for lymphoma
Failing to distinguish classic EATL from monomorphic epitheliotropic intestinal T-cell lymphoma, which differ in coeliac association and immunophenotype
Underestimating perforation risk when starting cytotoxic therapy
Overlooking profound malnutrition that limits treatment delivery
references: Swerdlow SH et al. WHO monograph on lymphoid neoplasms
management: Confirm diagnosis with immunophenotyping (CD3, CD103, CD4/CD8, CD30) and distinguish EATL from MEITL, which is CD8+/CD56+ and not celiac related
Stage as an aggressive lymphoma with cross-sectional and PET/CT imaging and bone marrow evaluation
Assess for celiac disease and refractory celiac disease with endoscopic and pathologic confirmation, plus baseline nutritional assessment
Perform urgent surgical resection when patients present with obstruction, perforation, or bleeding, which also provides diagnostic tissue
Recognize that surgery alone is not curative and systemic treatment should follow in patients fit enough to receive it
Give adjuvant anthracycline-based chemotherapy after resection
Consider CHOP-type combination chemotherapy as the general approach for aggressive T-cell lymphomas as a class
Consider a CD30-targeted antibody-drug conjugate combination for CD30-positive cases, extrapolated from PTCL data since EATL-specific trial data are not reported
Consider consolidation with autologous stem cell transplantation in first remission for eligible, fit patients, extrapolated from general PTCL practice
Encourage enrollment in a clinical trial given the overall poor prognosis of this lymphoma group

For relapsed or refractory disease, consider antifolate-based therapy, histone deacetylase inhibitor therapy, or allogeneic stem cell transplantation in selected patients, extrapolated from PTCL practice rather than EATL-specific evidence
Maintain strict adherence to a gluten-free diet as the approach to preventing progression from enteropathy to lymphoma, alongside ongoing management of refractory celiac disease
Follow with interval cross-sectional or PET imaging and ongoing surveillance for bowel complications such as obstruction, perforation, or bleeding
Refer promptly to a center with hematology-oncology expertise in T-cell lymphomas with concurrent gastroenterology involvement for celiac disease and nutritional management
